key_insight: Many state-of-the-art Video-LLMs are unable to reliably perceive signed image-plane motion (left/right/up/down): their above-chance answers often arise from dataset or prediction biases rather than true motion understanding—an effect the authors call "directional motion blindness."
problem_solved: Diagnoses and localizes a basic failure mode in temporal video understanding—signed motion direction—then proposes targeted interventions to detect and reduce this blindness so models truly perceive directional motion.
method: Construct controlled, minimal videos of a single object moving in one of four cardinal directions to isolate signed motion cues.
Systematically evaluate and probe multiple Video-LLMs to trace failure modes and attribute above-chance performance to prediction biases and non-motion cues.

Introduce corrective interventions (e.g., targeted finetuning/augmentation, explicit motion supervision such as optical-flow-based signals, and prompting strategies) to restore genuine direction perception.
impact: Fixing directional motion blindness improves core temporal perception in Video-LLMs, increasing reliability for downstream tasks that depend on true motion understanding (e.g., robotics, video QA, surveillance) and raising the bar for robust evaluation.
visual_elements: A 2x2 grid of minimal example videos (or frame sequences) with overlaid arrows indicating ground-truth motion directions (left/right/up/down).
Confusion matrix comparing model predictions vs. true directions to highlight chance-level performance and systematic biases.
Side-by-side attention/feature-map or optical-flow visualizations showing where models attend before and after mitigation.
Bar chart showing performance (accuracy) across models and the improvement after proposed interventions (augmentation/finetuning).
paper_title: Which Way Did It Move? Diagnosing and Overcoming Directional Motion Blindness in Video-LLMs
paper_authors: Jongseo Lee, Hyuntak Lee, Sunghun Kim, Sooa Kim, Jihoon Chung
